open_obligations: Check which design difference (hidden passage, interaction, baseline) explains the different conclusions.
Note that Michael et al. have no no-argument baseline, so the two results answer different comparisons.
Check that both use QuALITY questions of comparable difficulty (hard subsets).
in.other_title: Debate beats consultancy for non-expert human judges: 84% vs 74% on hard QuALITY questions
in.rationale: Parrish et al. conclude that, for reading comprehension, debate is not a helpful format, since judges perform similarly with or without two-turn arguments. Michael et al. report 84% judge accuracy for interactive human debate versus 74% for consultancy on QuALITY-hard; settings differ sharply: Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage, debates are interactive and unbounded, and the baseline is consultancy rather than no arguments.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate is a helpful format for human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension

open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51, where the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Check that Parrish et al.'s two-turn judges had time-limited passage access, unlike Michael et al.'s judges
Compare the baselines: Parrish et al. compare with a no-argument condition, Michael et al. with consultancy
in.other_title: Michael et al. find debate helps QuALITY judges, unlike Parrish et al.'s two-turn null result
in.rationale: Parrish et al.'s two-turn study (one argument plus one counter-argument) reports no accuracy gain, while Michael et al. report a positive debate result on the same dataset. The authors attribute the difference to their unbounded length, interaction and hidden-passage setup, and say absolute accuracies are not comparable, so the challenge is scoped to protocol.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether multi-turn debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the contrast depends on debate length, judge interaction and expertise gap

open_obligations: Note that two turns is still far from unbounded interactive debate.
Check that the judges, now selected Upwork workers with 5 minutes, are comparable to the original MTurk judges.
Check whether judges could read enough of the passage to bypass the arguments.
out.other_title: Is multi-turn debate with explicit counterarguments needed to help human judges?
out.rationale: Parrish et al. (single-turn) ask whether a multi-turn setting with counterarguments is needed. The two-turn follow-up adds counter-arguments (90% and 85% of which directly respond to the first argument) and reports human judges perform similarly with or without arguments, e.g. 72.8% vs 74.8% correct under simple incentives; judges had 5 minutes and passage access.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether adding explicit counter-arguments makes debate helpful to human judges, on 2-option QuALITY with human-written arguments

text: The authors test whether adding a second round of counter-arguments to single-turn debate arguments helps human judges answer hard multiple-choice reading comprehension questions, and report that humans perform similarly whether or not they have access to the arguments. They conclude that, for answering reading comprehension questions, debate is not a helpful format.
title: Two-turn debate with counter-arguments does not help humans answer hard QuALITY questions
